title: Rate limiting: algorithms and where they live
summary: Why and where to limit, token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed and sliding windows, 429 with Retry-After, sharing a limit across instances, and the .NET and Polly APIs seniors configure for it.

steps.title: Why limit, and where
body: A rate limit caps how much one caller may ask for. It exists to:
- **protect** the backend from spikes, bugs and abuse (a client stuck in a loop);
- keep things **fair** between tenants, so one big customer cannot starve the rest;
- control **cost** (an expensive search, a paid third-party API behind you).
Where it runs:
```text
client ──> CDN / edge ──> API gateway ──> service ──> dependency
per IP        per API key      per caller    the client side: stay under the
(abuse)       (plans, tenants)  (protect me)  partner's limit before they 429 you
Reject with **`429 Too Many Requests`** and a **`Retry-After`** header (seconds), so well-behaved clients wait
the right time. Many APIs also send remaining-quota headers; the IETF is standardising `RateLimit` headers,
but formats still differ between products, so document yours.

steps.prompt: Your public API sells plans: Free gets 10 requests per second, Pro gets 200, per API key. Where should that limit be enforced?
options: At the API gateway, partitioned by API key, before requests reach the services
In each backend service, by client IP address
In the database, with a connection limit
In the client SDK, trusting customers to call it
steps.explain: The gateway sees every request and the key that identifies the plan, and rejecting there costs almost nothing. IP addresses are shared (offices, mobile carriers) and spoofable for this purpose; client-side limits are a courtesy, not enforcement.

steps.title: Five algorithms
body: | Algorithm | How it works | Good at | Watch out |
| **Token bucket** | tokens refill at rate `r` up to capacity `b`; a request takes one | allows bursts up to `b`, average `r` | burst size is a real choice |
| **Leaky bucket** | requests join a queue drained at a fixed rate | perfectly smooth output | adds queueing delay; full queue rejects |
| **Fixed window** | count per calendar window (`12:00:00-12:00:59`) | one counter, trivial in Redis | up to 2x the limit across a window boundary |
| **Sliding window log** | keep every request's timestamp for the last window | exact | memory per request |
| **Sliding window counter** | `previous × (1 − elapsed/window) + current` | close to exact, two counters | an estimate, not exact |
Token bucket is the usual default for APIs: it lets a client send a short burst (page load) while holding
the average. Step through one with capacity 5 that refills 2 tokens a second.

steps.prompt: The same bucket: capacity 5, 2 tokens per second. Seven requests arrive at t=0 and three at t=1. What does this print?
steps.explain: At t=0 the full bucket lets 5 through and refuses 2. One second later 2 tokens have refilled: 2 more are accepted and the third is refused. 5 + 2 = 7.

steps.title: One limit, many instances
body: A limiter that counts in memory counts **per instance**. Twelve gateway pods with "100 per second" each let
a client through at up to 1,200 per second. Options:
- **A shared counter** in Redis: fixed window with `INCR` plus `EXPIRE` on a key like `rl:{apiKey}:{minute}`,
or a token bucket in a small Lua script so the read-modify-write is atomic. Costs one round trip per
request (sub-millisecond in the same zone).
- **Local limits divided by the instance count**, refreshed as you scale. No extra hop; rough when traffic
is uneven across pods.
- **Local plus periodic sync**: count locally, push and pull totals every few hundred ms.
Decide what happens when the shared store is down: **fail open** (allow traffic, protect availability) for
most APIs, **fail closed** where the limit guards money or abuse. Write it in the design.

steps.prompt: Match each algorithm to its behaviour.
pairs: Short bursts up to the capacity, then the refill rate
A queue drained at a constant rate: smooth output, added delay
Up to twice the limit around a window boundary
Exact, but stores a timestamp per request
Weights the previous window's count by how much of it still overlaps

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: rate limits and resilience in .NET
steps.body: The real APIs: ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware (in the box since .NET 7), Polly v8 resilience pipelines, and the standard resilience handler for HttpClient.

toolkit.what: Registers the rate limiting middleware with a named token bucket policy; endpoints opt in with `RequireRateLimiting`.
flags: reject at once instead of queueing

toolkit.what: One limiter per partition key (an API key, a tenant, a user), so each caller gets its own bucket.
A sliding window split into segments, so a window boundary cannot double the limit.
toolkit.example: o.AddSlidingWindowLimiter("search", w => { w.PermitLimit = 600; w.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1); w.SegmentsPerWindow = 6; w.QueueLimit = 0; });

toolkit.what: Runs when a request is rejected: the place to set `Retry-After` from the lease's metadata.
flags: how long until a permit is likely
toolkit.example: o.OnRejected = (ctx, ct) => { if (ctx.Lease.TryGetMetadata(MetadataName.RetryAfter, out var wait)) ctx.HttpContext.Response.Headers.RetryAfter = ((int)wait.TotalSeconds).ToString(); return ValueTask.CompletedTask; };
toolkit.when: every limiter that clients are expected to respect

toolkit.what: From `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`: adds a Polly pipeline to an HttpClient: rate limiter, total request timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, per-attempt timeout.
toolkit.example:
builder.Services.AddHttpClient("pricing", c => c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://pricing.example.com"))
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(o => { o.AttemptTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(350); o.TotalRequestTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1); });
toolkit.when: any outgoing HttpClient: start from the standard handler and tune its timeouts to your budget

toolkit.what: Polly v8: build your own pipeline of strategies, applied outside-in in the order added.
flags: a timeout around what follows it
toolkit.when: resilience around something that is not an HttpClient (a database call, a queue publish)

toolkit.what: A shared fixed-window counter: increment the key for this caller and minute, set it to expire, compare with the limit.
flags: atomically add one and return the new count
set a time to live only if none is set yet (Redis 7+)
toolkit.example: redis-cli INCR rl:key_3f9a:2026-11-27T14:05 && redis-cli EXPIRE rl:key_3f9a:2026-11-27T14:05 120 NX
toolkit.when: checking by hand what a shared limiter has counted

toolkit.what: Shows the status and headers, so you can see the 429 and its `Retry-After` and quota headers.
flags: only print the status, for a quick loop
toolkit.example: for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'X-Api-Key: test-key' https://api.example.com/orders; done | sort | uniq -c
toolkit.when: proving that a limit is really enforced, and at what rate

steps.prompt: Configure a token bucket that allows bursts of 100, refills 50 per second, rejects at once with the right status, and turn the middleware on.
steps.explain: The middleware rejects with 503 unless you say otherwise; 429 tells the client it is being limited rather than that the server is broken. `TokenLimit` is the bucket's capacity (`PermitLimit` belongs to the window limiters). Without `UseRateLimiter` nothing is enforced.

prompt: **Symptom first.** The contract says 100 requests per second per customer. The pricing backend fell over
during a customer's batch job, and the gateway logs show that customer at 1,150 requests per second with
almost no 429s. The gateway config:
code: limiter: in-memory token bucket per API key, TokenLimit 100, 100 per second
options: Each of the 12 replicas counts separately, so the real limit is about 1,200 per second: share the counter (Redis) or divide the limit by the replica count
The token bucket's capacity is too large: set it to 1
The customer is spoofing API keys
429 responses are being cached by the CDN
steps.explain: In-memory limits are per process. With 3 replicas the leak was 3x and nobody noticed; autoscaling to 12 made it 12x. A shared counter costs a sub-millisecond round trip; a local limit divided by the replica count must be updated whenever you scale.

steps.title: A token bucket with an injected clock
prompt: Write a class `TokenBucket` (time in seconds is passed in):
- `TokenBucket(double capacity, double refillPerSec)`: starts **full**;
- `bool TryTake(double nowSec, double cost = 1)`: refill first (`refillPerSec` per second since the last
call, never above `capacity`), then take `cost` tokens if there are enough;
- `double Tokens(double nowSec)`: refill, then return the tokens left;
- if `nowSec` is **earlier** than the last time seen (clocks do jump), do not refill and do not move the last
time backwards.
Capacity 5 at 2 per second: seven requests at t=0 give five `true` and two `false`; at t=1 two more pass.
starter: public bool TryTake(double nowSec, double cost = 1) => true;
solution: if (!started) { started = true; last = nowSec; return; }
public bool TryTake(double nowSec, double cost = 1)
hints: Keep the tokens and the last time; refill by `(now - last) × rate`, capped with `Math.Min`.
The very first call has nothing to refill from: just remember its time. A time earlier than `last` changes nothing.
template: var dojoTb = new TokenBucket(5, 2);
var dojoFirst = Enumerable.Range(0, 7).Select(_ => dojoTb.TryTake(0)).ToList();
Dojo.Eq("a full bucket passes a burst of 5, then refuses", new List<bool> { true, true, true, true, true, false, false }, dojoFirst);
var dojoSecond = Enumerable.Range(0, 3).Select(_ => dojoTb.TryTake(1)).ToList();
Dojo.Eq("one second later, two tokens have refilled", new List<bool> { true, true, false }, dojoSecond);
Dojo.Eq("empty now", 0.0, dojoTb.Tokens(1));
Dojo.Eq("refill never passes the capacity", 5.0, dojoTb.Tokens(10));
Dojo.Check("a request can cost more than one token", dojoTb.TryTake(10, 3));
Dojo.Eq("three were taken", 2.0, dojoTb.Tokens(10));
Dojo.Check("too expensive is refused", !dojoTb.TryTake(10, 3));
Dojo.Check("a clock that jumps back still works", dojoTb.TryTake(9));
Dojo.Eq("but refills nothing", 1.0, dojoTb.Tokens(10));
Dojo.Eq("half a second later: one more token", 2.0, dojoTb.Tokens(10.5));
Dojo.Eq("a new bucket starts full", 3.0, new TokenBucket(3, 1).Tokens(100));
{{CODE}}

steps.title: A sliding window counter
prompt: Write a class `SlidingWindowCounter` (time in ms is passed in):
- `SlidingWindowCounter(int limit, long windowMs)`;
- windows are aligned: the current one starts at `nowMs - nowMs % windowMs`;
- when a request falls into a new window, the old current count becomes the **previous** count if the new
window directly follows it, and `0` if one or more whole windows were skipped;
- `bool TryAcquire(long nowMs)`: estimate
`previous × (windowMs − elapsed) / windowMs + current`, where `elapsed` is the time since the current window
started. Accept (and count it) when `estimate + 1 <= limit`.
Limit 10 per 1,000 ms: ten requests at t=100 pass. At t=1500 half of the previous window still overlaps, so
it counts as 5 and only 5 more pass.
hints: Keep three numbers: the current window's start, its count, and the previous window's count.
Roll over when `nowMs - nowMs % windowMs` changes; the previous count survives only if exactly one window passed.
template: var dojoSw = new SlidingWindowCounter(10, 1000);
int dojoCount(long at, int tries) { var n = 0; for (var i = 0; i < tries; i++) if (dojoSw.TryAcquire(at)) n++; return n; }
Dojo.Eq("ten pass in the first window", 10, dojoCount(100, 12));
Dojo.Eq("at t=1500 the old window still counts as 5", 5, dojoCount(1500, 8));
Dojo.Eq("at t=2100 the previous 5 count as 4.5", 5, dojoCount(2100, 8));
Dojo.Eq("after skipped windows nothing carries over", 10, dojoCount(5000, 12));
var dojoFw = new SlidingWindowCounter(10, 1000);
var dojoEdge = 0;
for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (dojoFw.TryAcquire(999)) dojoEdge++;
for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (dojoFw.TryAcquire(1000)) dojoEdge++;
Dojo.Eq("no double burst across the boundary (a fixed window would allow 20)", 10, dojoEdge);
